Quoting, Summarizing, Paraphrasing
Introduction

This module explores three standard methods for integrating outside sources in your writing—quoting, summarizing, and paraphrasing. 
The reason for using outside sources is to support, deepen, reflect, contradict, or otherwise enhance your own ideas.
This module requires your careful reading and thoughtful consideration.
Investigate each method.
Examine each method by exploring the source text, tips for writing, and the sample rewrite.
Working with the Source Text
You will be working in this module with one source text, which allows us to compare the three methods and allows you, the writer, to work closely with a single passage.

The source text below is a single paragraph from a 13-page journal article, "'It Wasn't Me, Was It?' Plagiarism and the Web," by D. DeVoss & A. C. Rosati, 2002, Computers and Composition, 19, 191-203. Click here to see the full article.
SOURCE TEXT

Two beliefs scaffold this article: First, we are witnessing students adapting their literacy, research, reading, and writing skills and processes to the virtual space—and complexity—of the World Wide Web. Second, first-year composition teachers have a key role in helping students adapt to this space, and encouraging students' critical research and writing skills in this space. Although students enter our classrooms well versed in writing-related values and ideas relayed to them in their past school experiences, often this instruction does not address—or does not go far enough in addressing—issues of online research and writing. First-year composition seems, to us, to be the ideal place to initiate discussions related to such issues; first-year composition courses tackle (among many other functions) the task of acculturating students into academic writing. Because academic writing now relies so heavily on the reading, writing, and research accessed via virtual spaces, it is necessary for first-year composition courses to address research and writing in electronic realms and to help students develop techniques that will aid them to best use these systems. From this perspective, we address the intersections of online research and plagiarism, discuss how we can best handle plagiarism in our first-year classrooms, and how we can best equip students with the tools necessary to do appropriate research—both online and offline. (p. 193)
Topic
"Two beliefs scaffold this article:"
Topic Expanded

"First, we are witnessing students adapting their literacy, research, reading, and writing skills and processes to the virtual space—and complexity—of the World Wide Web. Second, first-year composition teachers have a key role in helping students adapt to this space, and encouraging students' critical research and writing skills in this space."
Supporting Details

"…students enter our classrooms well versed in writing-related values and ideas…instruction does not address—or does not go far enough in addressing—issues of online research and writing. First-year composition…ideal place to initiate discussions related to such issues; first-year composition…acculturating students into academic writing.…academic writing now relies so heavily on the reading, writing, and research accessed via virtual spaces…address research and writing in electronic realms and to help students develop techniques that will aid them to best use these systems."
Summary

"From this perspective, we address the intersections of online research and plagiarism, discuss how we can best handle plagiarism in our first-year classrooms, and how we can best equip students with the tools necessary to do appropriate research—both online and offline."

In every work you use in your research, you will need to identify the main points, supporting details, and passages that stand out as essential. You may not know immediately whether you will directly quote, summarize, or paraphrase the material, but as you refine your topic and thesis, you will be better placed to identify ideas and text you might want to use in your paper.
We will be exploring all three methods using this source text, starting with a direct quotation.
Direct Quoting
Overview
To directly quote means to reproduce another writer's text verbatim.
A direct quotation must be thoughtfully selected. The DK Handbook (2011) speaks well to this point:

When you quote the words of others, it is as though you invite the words to speak for you: You bring both the sense of speaking and the authority of the speaker into your writing. Because of this, use the exact words of others in your writing when those words add something to your argument that you cannot provide with your own words. (p. 300)
Choosing to quote
Ask yourself, Does the quoted text enhance my point in a way that paraphrasing or summarizing the same passage would not?
Ask yourself, Does the original language carry more weight than would using my own words?
Use direct quotations thoughtfully and judiciously. Some assignments or types of writing may require direct quotations, while some instructors may limit their use.
Drafting Your quotation
Match the source text word for word and use the same punctuation; refer to APA 6.06.
Do not drop a direct quotation into your text without discussing it.
Include introductory and signal words/phrases.
Use past tense verbs for an action that has already occurred, such as when discussing what an author reported or wrote (refer to APA 3.18).
Format the quotation based on word length, as discussed and illustrated in APA 6.03.
Quoting Tips
Do not force a direct quote to agree with your viewpoint by misquoting or quoting out of context.
Cite author, date, and page number (if a work is not paginated, refer to APA 6.05).
Refer to APA 6.03 regarding how to punctuate a quotation.
Refer to APA 6.07–6.08 regarding changes from the source.

SOURCE TEXT

Two beliefs scaffold this article: First, we are witnessing students adapting their literacy, research, reading, and writing skills and processes to the virtual space—and complexity—of the World Wide Web. Second, first-year composition teachers have a key role in helping students adapt to this space, and encouraging students' critical research and writing skills in this space. Although students enter our classrooms well versed in writing-related values and ideas relayed to them in their past school experiences, often this instruction does not address—or does not go far enough in addressing—issues of online research and writing. From this perspective, we address the intersections of online research and plagiarism, discuss how we can best handle plagiarism in our first-year classrooms, and how we can best equip students with the tools necessary to do appropriate research—both online and offline. Computers and Composition 19 (2002) 191-203
QUOTING: EXAMPLE

DeVoss and Rosati's (2002) audience is first-year composition teachers, whom the authors recognize as key figures in helping students negotiate ethical online research and writing. The authors write that first-year composition courses are "ideal" for addressing techniques with which students can learn to recognize and navigate "the intersections of online research and plagiarism" (p. 193).

In this sample, a direct quotation is woven into a summary. The quoted text ("intersections of online research and plagiarism") acknowledges the audience for the article and observes the significant role first-year composition teachers hold in the post-secondary experience. The source text discusses more than plagiarism, of course, but the quoted text focuses on one of the key issues of ethical scholarship—how to research and write while understanding what plagiarism truly is and how to avoid it.

There is no "perfect" quotation in any source, and you may well have selected a different excerpt to support the argument. Your choice of quoted text will depend on your purpose and the source text itself.
Why this quotation works:
The quoted text speaks to a challenge that many writers face: how to avoid plagiarism when working with online sources (plagiarizing is inherently easy when copying and pasting text).
Authors DeVoss and Rosati have expertise in the field of first-year composition, so their words lend authority in a way that ours cannot.
The direct quotation fits into the paragraph grammatically and logically.
The quoted text matches the source text exactly.
Each piece of the quoted text begins and ends with double quotation marks.
The period that ends the sentence follows the page citation, not the quoted text (refer to APA 6.03).
Quoting: Practice
PRACTICE 1: Extending the audience for the direct quote
INSTRUCTIONS

Imagine you are writing an essay about the need for all teachers and students—not just those in a first-year composition course—to be adept at online research. Select the sentence that best integrates your imaginary essay topic of a wider audience and DeVoss and Rosati's call for solid online research skills?
CHOICE A

DeVoss and Rosati (2002, p. 193) remind us that "because academic writing now relies so heavily on the reading, writing, and research accessed via virtual spaces, it is necessary" for all students to learn the skills of academic writing.
cells.D: Although DeVoss and Rosati's (2002) article is geared to first-year composition teachers, their observation that educators "are witnessing students adapting their literacy, research, reading, and writing skills and processes to the virtual space—and complexity—of the World Wide Web" (p. 193) can be applied to nontraditional students, transfer students, and first-year graduate students just as well.

cells.C: Ineffective. A direct quotation should be used when it enhances your point in a way that paraphrasing or summarizing would not. It must provide a sense of the other authors' style and tone. Although the direct quotation in this example does include a signal phrase, in the words "remind us," it is more of a statement of fact than a crucial insight from DeVoss and Rosati.
cells.D: Effective. This direct quotation acknowledges that the audience for DeVoss and Rosati's article is first-year composition teachers, but it extends the audience to all students. The quotation addresses the difficulty of learning or relearning academic skills; this acknowledgment of the complex nature of scholarly reading and writing in an online environment is missing in Choice A. Choice B speaks about the need for all teachers and students to be adept at online research in a way that Choice A does not.

cells.C: PRACTICE 2: Using a direct quotation to support another source
INSTRUCTIONS

Imagine you are writing a short piece on the significance of the First Course experience as a means to understanding academic honesty in the university setting. This example asks that you first read the following excerpt from the Rationale section of University Policy 3.01.01, which addresses academic honesty:

In support of Capella University's core values, this policy establishes the standards for academic integrity and enforces the university's commitment to teaching and learning while maintaining academic integrity, authenticity, ethics, and scholarship in one's work as a learner at the university. This policy also establishes the due process procedures for the internal resolution of acts of academic dishonesty.

After reading this excerpt from the university policy, select the direct quotation from DeVoss and Rosati from the choices below that best support the idea that initial college experience—whether it be first-year composition or a First Course experience—must set the stage for academic integrity.
CHOICE A

Because academic writing now relies so heavily on the reading, writing, and research accessed via virtual spaces, it is necessary for first-year composition courses to address research and writing in electronic realms and to help students develop techniques that will aid them to best use these systems. (DeVoss & Rosati, 2002, p. 193)
cells.D: From this perspective, we address the intersections of online research and plagiarism, discuss how we can best handle plagiarism in our first-year classrooms, and how we can best equip students with the tools necessary to do appropriate research—both online and offline. (DeVoss & Rosati, 2002, p. 193)

cells.C: Effective. Although academic integrity is not mentioned specifically, this quotation does discuss how to support students in their academic journey, as in a First Course. The phrases "virtual spaces" and "electronic realms" apply to Capella's online learning environment. The statement about developing techniques for research and writing applies to an introductory online course, as well.
cells.D: Ineffective. This direct quotation focuses more on plagiarism than on other aspects of academic integrity. For this reason alone, the quotation only partially supports the premise that the first-year composition or a First Course experience should set the stage for academic integrity. On the other hand, this quotation would work well if the premise of the question had to do solely with original writing and/or plagiarism.

cells.C: PRACTICE 3: Punctuating and citing a direct quotation
When you take notes on your readings, make sure you have copied verbatim text exactly. This question asks you to compare a sentence against the source text and then write and cite it accurately.
INSTRUCTIONS

The sentence below needs to be punctuated correctly. (a) Rewrite the sentence so it contains the exact wording and punctuation of the original. (b) At the end of the quotation, cite the source in APA style.
Second, first year composition teachers have a key role in helping students adapt to this space and encouraging students critical research and writing skills in this space.
Answer

"Second, first-year composition teachers have a key role in helping students adapt to this space, and encouraging students' critical research and writing skills in this space" (DeVoss & Rosati, 2002, p. 193).
Your answer must demonstrate the following corrections:
Punctuation marks (hyphen, comma, apostrophe) match the source text (APA 6.06).
Quotation marks are placed around the verbatim text (APA 6.03).
Author-date citation and page number are separated by commas and placed in parentheses (APA 6.03).
The period that ends the sentence follows the citation, not the quotation (APA 6.03).
Summarizing
Overview
To summarize means to rewrite the main points of a passage in your own words.
An effective summary statement must be concisely focused on the author's key points as they relate to your own purpose in writing. The DK Handbook (2011) speaks well to these points:

When you summarize, you leave out illustrations, examples, and details not necessary for your arguments: Go for the main points.... [Also note] what the summary does not do: The summary's words do not repeat the exact words used in the excerpt. (p. 306)
Choosing to Summarize
Ask yourself, Are there key points, process steps, or other information in the original source text that I can condense?
Ask yourself, Can I condense or summarize the main points without misrepresenting the purpose of the original passage?
Ask yourself, Would a detailed paraphrase be a better way to present the material? Would a direct quotation add meaning and significance?
Drafting your Summary
Use the five steps of the Cornell method—record, reduce, recite, reflect, review—to guide your writing.
Put aside your draft for as much time as you need so you can return to it with objectivity.
Use past tense verbs for an action that has already occurred, such as when discussing what an author reported or wrote (refer to APA 3.18).
Summarizing Tips
Read the source text as often as needed, marking the text to identify the main points.
Do not distort the source text or inject your own bias and thus misrepresent or misinterpret what the other author has written.
Restate the source text in your own words and with your own voice and style. (Note: Removing a few words of the source text and replacing them with your own does not constitute a summary.)
Include only the main points of the passage in your summary.
Do a word count; your summary should be shorter than the passage.
Cite the author and date of the source; refer to APA 6.11–6.21.
Some instructors and mentors might require a page citation for a summary. Know the requirements of your assignment. Also refer to APA 6.04.

SOURCE TEXT

Two beliefs scaffold this article: First, we are witnessing students adapting their literacy, research, reading, and writing skills and processes to the virtual space—and complexity—of the World Wide Web. Second, first-year composition teachers have a key role in helping students adapt to this space, and encouraging students' critical research and writing skills in this space. Although students enter our classrooms well versed in writing-related values and ideas relayed to them in their past school experiences, often this instruction does not address—or does not go far enough in addressing—issues of online research and writing. First-year composition seems, to us, to be the ideal place to initiate discussions related to such issues; first-year composition courses tackle (among many other functions) the task of acculturating students into academic writing. Because academic writing now relies so heavily on the reading, writing, and research accessed via virtual spaces, it is necessary for first-year composition courses to address research and writing in electronic realms and to help students develop techniques that will aid them to best use these systems. From this perspective, we address the intersections of online research and plagiarism, discuss how we can best handle plagiarism in our first-year classrooms, and how we can best equip students with the tools necessary to do appropriate research—both online and offline. (p. 193)
SUMMARY: EXAMPLE

DeVoss and Rosati (2002) pointed out that students have come to rely on the virtual space of the Internet, and this reliance impacts how they engage in research. The authors called on first-year composition teachers to address the complex issues that electronic research engenders, particularly how to write critically about sources and how to avoid plagiarism. A first-year composition course, asserted the authors, is the best place to help students navigate the virtual space in which academic research and writing now reside.
Why this summary works:
The sentences highlighted in the source text cover the main points used in the summary example.

It restates the essence of the source: that the Internet has altered student research and that first-year composition teachers can be a resource for helping students avoid problems such as plagiarism.
It is written in the writer's own words.
It is shorter than the source text.
It cites the author and date of the source.
Practice
The following multiple-choice and short-answer activities provide practice in summarizing.
PRACTICE 1: Identifying effective summary statements
INSTRUCTIONS
Read the following sentence from DeVoss and Rosati, in which they describe what their article does. From the three choices that follow, choose the best summary of this sentence.

From this perspective, we address the intersections of online research and plagiarism, discuss how we can best handle plagiarism in our first-year classrooms, and how we can best equip students with the tools necessary to do appropriate research—both online and offline.
CHOICE A
DeVoss and Rosati (2002) addressed how to conduct online research and avoid plagiarism.
cells.D: DeVoss and Rosati (2002) discussed how teachers can avoid the hazards of online research and plagiarism in their first-year classes and best equip students with the tools for conducting appropriate research.
cells.E: DeVoss and Rosati (2002) described ways teachers can provide first-year students with strategies for avoiding plagiarism while they conduct both electronic and hard-copy research.

cells.C: Ineffective. This summary omits crucial information about the study, including any mention of the teachers, the students, and the learning experience.
cells.D: Ineffective. This summary does have two key elements of a successful summary: It includes the crucial points of and is shorter than the original. However, the wording adheres too closely to the source text. In particular, these pieces of text were copied from the original: "online research and plagiarism," "best handle plagiarism," "best equip students with the tools," "appropriate research."
cells.E: Effective. This summary captures the student-teacher learning experience and succinctly describes the purpose of the study. Also note that the source is cited.

cells.C: PRACTICE 2: Using a summary to establish the validity of the original source

Whether reading or writing scholarly and academic materials, you must have a sense of the author's credibility. That is, if you will be relying on the findings from a given author, you must ensure that the work merits being read, analyzed, and cited. Instances in which such a summary would be useful include:
an annotated bibliography.
a persuasive essay.
a literature review.
a response piece.
INSTRUCTIONS

Imagine you are writing about the challenges of your first online research and writing assignment. You plan to use DeVoss and Rosati's article as a source. Reading DeVoss and Rosati's entire article, you learn that:
The authors are first-year composition teachers.
Their abstract states that the purpose of their article is to share "experiences common to most teachers of writing."
The article was published in Computers and Composition, a professional journal for which the mission is, among other things, publishing research articles on computers in writing classes.

In the text box, use the sentence stems to write about adapting one's skills to the online environment: Acknowledge the authors' credibility by using information from the bulleted clues above, and summarize the following excerpt from DeVoss and Rosati:

Two beliefs scaffold this article: First, we are witnessing students adapting their literacy, research, reading, and writing skills and processes to the virtual space—and complexity—of the World Wide Web. Second, first-year composition teachers have a key role in helping students adapt to this space, and encouraging students' critical research and writing skills in this space.
DeVoss and Rosati (2002), who _______________, stated that _________________.
Drawing on their expertise/familiarity/experience in ______________, DeVoss and Rosati (2002) asserted/advocated/called for ______________.
ANSWER
Two examples are provided below for each sentence. Note that these are not the only ways this activity can be written.
Sentence 1 Examples

DeVoss and Rosati (2002), who are both first-year composition teachers, stated that first-year composition teachers must assist students as they begin to navigate the online learning environment and must support the students in developing the required scholarly skills.

DeVoss and Rosati (2002), who have observed in their classrooms that first-year students must ramp up their online academic skills, stated that first-year composition teachers, such as themselves, are well placed to assist and support students in this endeavor.
Sentence 2 Examples

Drawing on their familiarity in first-year composition classrooms, DeVoss and Rosati (2002) called for writing teachers to be cognizant of students' challenges and need for support in the online learning environment.

Drawing on their experience in observing first-year students begin the sometimes challenging academic journey, DeVoss and Rosati (2002) asserted that they hold two beliefs for first-year composition teachers: Teachers must carefully attend to students as they engage in the online learning environment, and they must support students in strengthening their academic rigor.
Note
There is no single correct answer, so make sure your summary adheres to the definition of and criteria for a good summary.
Does it encapsulate only the main point(s)?
Have you correctly interpreted the authors' text?
Is it shorter than the original?
Is it in your own words?
Have you cited author and date?
For more on evaluating source quality, see https://campus.capella.edu/web/library/library-research-skills/evaluating-source-quality
Paraphrasing
Overview

Paraphrasing well is challenging. In the researching and drafting phases, paraphrasing is an excellent tool for ensuring that you fully understand another writer's ideas, and also to make sure you aren't plagiarizing.
The DK Handbook (2011) offers this advice:

Paraphrase when you do not want to quote someone else's words, perhaps because you already have used many quotations or because the original words are not memorable or need modification so that your audience will understand them. (p. 308)

Present the ideas of another as you think that writer wants others to understand them—don't offer your interpretation or any comments until after you have finished a full and honest paraphrase. (p. 309)
Choosing to Paraphrase
Ask yourself, Would a summary be more appropriate? Would a direct quotation be more effective?
Ask yourself, What is the author's message? What do I, the writer, need to take away from the passage?
Ask yourself, What do my readers need to know?
Drafting your Paraphrase
Use the steps of the Cornell method—record, recite, reflect, review—to provide a structure for comparing your paraphrased text against the source text.
Put aside your draft for as much time as you need so you can return to it with objectivity.
Use past tense verbs for an action that has already occurred, such as when discussing what an author reported or wrote (refer to APA 3.18).
Paraphrasing Tips
Read the source text as often as needed, marking the text to identify the main points and supporting details.
Do not distort the source text or inject your own bias and thus misrepresent or misinterpret what the other author has written.
Do not include your own opinion or evaluation in the paraphrase.

Change the sentence structure and use your own wording, but do not change the overall order of ideas of the source text. (Note: Removing a few words of the source text and replacing them with your own is not paraphrasing.)
Do a word count; your paraphrase should be about the same length as or longer than the passage.
Cite the author and date of the source; refer to APA 6.11–6.21.
Some instructors and mentors might require a page citation for a paraphrase. Know the requirements of your assignment. Also refer to APA 6.04.

SOURCE TEXT

Two beliefs scaffold this article: First, we are witnessing students adapting their literacy, research, reading, and writing skills and processes to the virtual space—and complexity—of the World Wide Web. Second, first-year composition teachers have a key role in helping students adapt to this space, and encouraging students' critical research and writing skills in this space. PARAPHRASE: EXAMPLE

DeVoss and Rosati (2002), in their article "'It Wasn't Me, Was It?' Plagiarism and the Web," concede that although first-year college students bring previous writing experience, traditional instruction no longer adequately prepares students as they navigate the obstacles inherent in researching and writing in virtual space.
Why this paraphrase works:

You might need to paraphrase a single sentence when your assignment restricts the use of direct quotations, when a paraphrase fits into the sentence better than a direct quotation would, or when you are balancing your own findings with those from another researcher.
The paraphrase includes the main points and the key supporting details of the source.

The primary purpose of the source text is to describe the problem with the current state of writing instruction. The overall order of ideas and information has not been changed. However, the sentence structure and wording have been changed.
The paraphrase includes the authors and date, both essential components of the source citation.
This example also includes the title of the article; the title is not required but can be useful to provide context for the paraphrase.
The paraphrase is slightly longer than the source text.
Practice
PRACTICE 1: Distinguishing between paraphrasing and plagiarism

Of the three methods—direct quotation, summary, and paraphrase—paraphrasing can be the most technically difficult. It requires an understanding of the original source and of your own purpose for paraphrasing, and it requires a careful attention to detail. A paraphrase that adheres too closely to the original text can border on or in fact be plagiarism.
INSTRUCTIONS
Read the following sentence from the source text, and from the choices below that does not contain plagiarized text.

Although students enter our classrooms well versed in writing-related values and ideas relayed to them in their past school experiences, often this instruction does not address—or does not go far enough in addressing—issues of online research and writing.
CHOICE A

Even though students are well aware of the writing-related values and ideas they have learned in past school experiences, DeVoss and Rosati (2002) purported that students' previous instruction did not cover or go far enough in covering the problems of online research and writing. .
cells.D: DeVoss and Rosati (2002) acknowledged that their students had received instruction on writing-related values and ideas in their past school experience, but that the instruction failed to successfully address issues of online research and writing.
cells.E: DeVoss and Rosati (2002) observed that their students have retained solid understanding of writing-related concepts learned in previous academic coursework, yet they observe as well that students evidence gaps in knowledge regarding researching and writing in the electronic environment.

cells.C: Ineffective. This paraphrase includes several word units that match the original text exactly: "writing-related values and ideas," "past school experiences," and "online research and writing." The unit "did not cover or go far enough in covering" matches the phrasing of "does not address—or does not go far enough in addressing" while merely changing the verb address to cover. Another error in this paraphrase is the use of the verb purported: Purport means to put forth as true, or to falsely claim, so writers should not use purport when they mean assert.
cells.D: Ineffective. This paraphrase includes three word units that match the original text exactly: "writing-related values and ideas," "past school experience," "issues of online research and writing." Also, the paraphrase misrepresents the original sentence in that it introduces the idea that the students' previous education was in some way a failure; the original sentence indicates that the previous instruction may not have gone as deeply as is now required in post-secondary education, but the original does not give any indication of failure.
cells.E: Effective. This paraphrase captures the key points of the original sentence, is about the same length as the original sentence, and is written in the writer's own words. Also note that the source is cited.

cells.C: PRACTICE 2: Integrating a paraphrase with your own ideas

DeVoss and Rosati indicate that first-year composition courses are the ideal setting for "acculturating students into academic writing." However, perhaps you know of other settings that would work just as well. Perhaps you feel that students should already have these skills or should learn by doing. Or perhaps you have entirely different thoughts.
INSTRUCTIONS
Complete the sentence stems below by writing a short paraphrase of this sentence from DeVoss and Rosati and then integrating your own ideas:

First-year composition seems, to us, to be the ideal place to initiate discussions related to such issues; first-year composition courses tackle (among many other functions) the task of acculturating students into academic writing.
DeVoss and Rosati (2002) observed that ____________________. However, my experience has been/I have observed/I believe that ____________________.
ANSWER
Three sample answers are provided below. Note that these are not the only ways this activity can be written.
Example 1

DeVoss and Rosati (2002) observed that a vital component of first-year composition classrooms is students' exploration of virtual literacy. However, I have observed that the discussion can be more theoretical than practical.
Example 2

DeVoss and Rosati (2002) observed that one main goal of first-year composition teachers is to instill awareness of the academic writing process in their students. However, I believe that post-secondary and graduate students should demonstrate those skills before enrolling.
Example 3

DeVoss and Rosati (2002) observed that the first-year composition classroom provides students with opportunities to engage in all aspects of academic writing. However, my experience has been that it was helpful for me to supplement the classroom experience with one-on-one tutoring.
Note
There is no single correct answer, so make sure your paraphrase adheres to the definition of and criteria for a good paraphrase.
Is it written in your own voice and style?
Have you covered the important details?
Have you correctly interpreted the source text?
Have you cited the source?
PRACTICE 3: Practicing paraphrasing
You previously practiced writing summary statements for the excerpt below, and now you will be paraphrasing it. When you are done, compare your paraphrase with your summary.
INSTRUCTIONS
Write a paraphrase of the following text from DeVoss and Rosati's article.

Two beliefs scaffold this article: First, we are witnessing students adapting their literacy, research, reading, and writing skills and processes to the virtual space—and complexity—of the World Wide Web. Second, first-year composition teachers have a key role in helping students adapt to this space, and encouraging students' critical research and writing skills in this space.
ANSWER
A sample answer is provided below. Note that this is not the only way this activity can be written.

DeVoss and Rosati (2002) discussed the two assumptions that guided their article "'It Wasn't Me, Was It?' Plagiarism and the Web." Their first assumption is that first-year composition teachers directly observe how virtual space (e.g., the Internet) affects student literacy in reading, researching, and writing. The authors' second assumption is that the first-year composition classroom lends itself well to assisting students as they explore best practices for critical writing, practices that will support the students in their college education.
Note
There is no single correct answer, so make sure your paraphrase adheres to the definition of and criteria for a good paraphrase.
Is it written in your own voice and style?
Have you covered the important details?
Have you correctly interpreted the source text?
Have you cited the source?
Is your paraphrase about the same length as or longer than the original?

A useful exercise is to compare the summary and paraphrase you wrote side by side. Does each fulfill the definition of and criteria for a summary and paraphrase? Each method will become easier as you gain more writing experience.

Provide citations for data sets when you have either conducted secondary analyses of publicly archived data or archived your own data being presented for the first time in the current work.
If you are citing existing data or statistics, cite the publication in which the data were published (e.g., a journal article, report, or webpage) rather than the data set itself.
The date in the reference is the year of publication for the version of the data used.
Provide the title of the data set in italics. Then provide any numerical identifier and version number for the data in parentheses without italics, separated by a semicolon.
The bracketed description is flexible (e.g., “[Data set],” “[Data set and code book]”).
Provide the publisher of the data set in the source element. ICPSR is one common example.
